newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH PM VOTE WIN PROVIDES LITTLE BOOST TO MARKETS.
newsitem.headline: CZECH PM VOTE WIN PROVIDES LITTLE BOOST TO MARKETS.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's narrow confidence vote win provided little boost to the country's capital markets on Wednesday, with analysts saying a win for the premier's coalition was already built into prices.
The crown weakened slightly at the opening of trading, but then steadied at late Tuesday levels of about 18.7 against the mark and 32.2 against the dollar.
Czech shares were steady at the Prague Stock Exchange's daily price fixing, with moderate gains to a few blue chip issues pushing the PX50 index up 0.51 percent to 508.9.
"We started with a quiet market. I think the (Klaus) win was expected so it did not affect the market too much," Jan Strupek, a forex trader at Komercni Banka told Reuters.

Klaus's government squeaked through a vote of confidence late on Tuesday, winning endorsement of his rescue plan for the economy and crown only after 11th hour negotiations culminating in a promise to give parliament a say in key bank and utility privatisations.

Analysts had widely predicted the victory before it was taken and said it was now up to the government to deliver on the promises it has made to reform the capital markets, restructure companies and push on with privatisation if there is to be a sustainable uptrend.
"Now it is time to get back to work and clean up the markets, stop corruption...it is the government's job to do this," said Jan Sykora an equities trader at Wood and Company.

Klaus had called for the confidence test on the cabinet's plans for budget cuts to counter an economic downturn and sharp depreciation in the Czech crown. If he had lost he would have been forced to resign.
The vote had seemed safe for Klaus when a Communist deputy, Miroslav Vacek, announced he was too ill to take part.
But Vacek showed up just before voting began, putting the onus for the government's survival on independent deputy Jozef Wagner, who is chairman of the budget committee. .
Wagner had his price -- demanding that the house get a say on privatisations of major banks and utilities proposed by the Finance Ministry.
Klaus rejected that demand just minutes before the vote -- then, when Vacek arrived, held a hasty meeting with Wagner and announced that the cabinet would submit the privatisations to the house.
Some dealers stressed that although the market would be pleased with the result of the vote, nothing fundamental had changed because of it.
"They've just got to start delivering. Because of this vote it does not mean interest rates are any lower or companies are better restructured," said one local dealer who requested anonymity.
The government's latest crisis economic plans will cut the 1997 budget by 20 billion crowns in an effort to check domestic demand and reduce a huge current account deficit.

In April the government, under a wave of criticism for a slumping economy and opaque capital markets, announced budget cuts of 25.5 billion crowns, and a series of measures aimed at shoring up market regulation and spurring economic growth.
But, warned some analysts, the government is still fragile, and with a long road ahead, is in for more turmoil.

"Given the recent history of the coalition, the odds are, however, that the lack of team spirit that has been typical for this coalition government will soon emerge again," said Prague- based political analyst Jiri Pehe.
